entradas.texto:
[i]Logbook note: you picked the same ship that made history.[/i]

On July 16, 1969, a [color=#f5c542]Saturn V[/color] rocket thundered off the pad carrying three astronauts toward the Moon. While [color=#8fd3ff]Michael Collins[/color] circled overhead in the command module [b]Columbia[/b], [color=#8fd3ff]Neil Armstrong[/color] and [color=#8fd3ff]Buzz Aldrin[/color] steered the lunar module [b]Eagle[/b] down to the [color=#f5c542]Sea of Tranquility[/color]. Seconds before touchdown, Armstrong took manual control to dodge a boulder-filled crater, landing about four miles off target with very little fuel to spare. Around 650 million people watched him step onto the surface and say: [i]“That's one small step for a man, one giant leap for mankind.”[/i]

The crew took a phone call from then-President Richard Nixon and left behind a silicon disk with goodwill messages from 73 countries. Riding a [color=#f5c542]free-return trajectory[/color], a cosmic slingshot that would have swung them home even if the engine failed, they traveled 953,054 miles in 8 days, 3 hours and 18 minutes before splashing down safely in the Pacific.

[i]Logbook note: your crew is flying the newest chapter of the Moon story.[/i]

In April 2026, the [color=#f5c542]SLS[/color] rocket launched the [b]Orion[/b] spacecraft on its first flight with people aboard: a nearly 10-day loop around the Moon. NASA astronauts [color=#8fd3ff]Reid Wiseman[/color], [color=#8fd3ff]Victor Glover[/color] and [color=#8fd3ff]Christina Koch[/color], together with Canadian Space Agency astronaut [color=#8fd3ff]Jeremy Hansen[/color], traveled [color=#f5c542]252,756 miles[/color] from Earth, the farthest humans have ever gone, and saw parts of the lunar surface that no human eyes had seen before.

On April 4, more than two-thirds of the way to the Moon, Commander Wiseman looked back through one of Orion's cabin windows and photographed home: a small, bright Earth floating in the dark. Artemis II is the dress rehearsal for the missions that will put astronauts back on the lunar surface.

[i]Logbook note: before anyone could walk on the Moon, someone had to learn to walk in space.[/i]

Gemini IV lifted off on June 3, 1965, for a four-day mission that set a new American record for time in space. High above Hawaii, [color=#8fd3ff]Ed White[/color] opened the hatch and floated outside, tied to the capsule by a 25-foot, gold-wrapped [color=#f5c542]umbilical cord[/color], while [color=#8fd3ff]Jim McDivitt[/color] took photos from inside. It was the [color=#f5c542]first American spacewalk[/color]. White steered himself with a handheld oxygen [i]“zip gun”[/i] and spent about 20 minutes drifting over the Earth. [i]“You look beautiful, Ed,”[/i] McDivitt radioed. [i]“I feel like a million dollars,”[/i] White replied, and when he was ordered back inside he called it [i]“the saddest moment of my life.”[/i]

The crew also practiced navigating by the stars with a [color=#f5c542]sextant[/color], completed 62 orbits and splashed down in the Atlantic, where the USS Wasp picked them up. Every Apollo moonwalk built on what they learned.

entradas.subtitulo_o_fecha: A layer cake made of air
entradas.texto:
[i]Logbook note: you just punched through all five layers. Here's what you flew through.[/i]

Earth's atmosphere wraps the planet like a giant, invisible layer cake. It gives us air to breathe, blocks harmful [color=#f5c542]UV rays[/color] and keeps temperatures livable. Without it we would swing like the Moon, from -208 °F to 250 °F. The planes, balloons, meteors and satellites you dodged on the way up each belong to one of its layers.

First comes the [color=#8fd3ff]troposphere[/color], where all our weather happens. Next is the [color=#8fd3ff]stratosphere[/color], home of airliners and the protective [color=#f5c542]ozone layer[/color]. The freezing [color=#8fd3ff]mesosphere[/color] is where most meteors burn up. The [color=#8fd3ff]thermosphere[/color] can heat past 2,000 °C; the International Space Station orbits there, and the [color=#f5c542]auroras[/color] glow inside it. Last is the [color=#8fd3ff]exosphere[/color], where the air thins out until its final molecules drift away into space.

[i]Logbook note: the storm that sent your crew into the shelter started here.[/i]

About every 11 years the Sun reaches [color=#f5c542]solar maximum[/color]. Tangled magnetic fields on its surface snap and reconnect, unleashing huge explosions called [color=#f5c542]solar flares[/color], often together with giant clouds of charged particles known as [color=#f5c542]coronal mass ejections[/color] (CMEs). Flares are ranked A, B, C, M and X, and each letter packs 10 times more energy than the one before. The biggest, [color=#8fd3ff]X-class[/color] flares, are the largest explosions in the solar system, releasing as much energy as a billion hydrogen bombs.

In 2003 a flare was so strong that it overloaded NASA's sensors; scientists later estimated it at [color=#8fd3ff]X28[/color]. In 2006, X-class flares disrupted GPS signals around the globe. When a storm points at Earth, its radiation can threaten astronauts, satellites and power grids, so NASA and NOAA watch the Sun day and night to warn crews in time to take cover.

[i]Logbook note: the Moon, up close at last. Its surface remembers everything.[/i]

The Moon is a cosmic [color=#f5c542]time capsule[/color]. On Earth, wind, water and moving tectonic plates erase old scars, but the Moon keeps the marks of the violent collisions that shaped the solar system. When an asteroid or comet slams into it, the impact blasts out shattered rock called [color=#f5c542]ejecta[/color]. Small hits leave bowl-shaped [color=#8fd3ff]simple craters[/color]; bigger ones form [color=#8fd3ff]complex craters[/color] with central peaks and terraced walls; the largest carve [color=#8fd3ff]impact basins[/color] more than 186 miles wide.

Billions of years ago, magma rose through cracks beneath those giant basins and cooled into dark, smooth plains of basalt called [color=#f5c542]maria[/color], Latin for “seas.” They are the dark patches that form the familiar “face” we see in the night sky.
